:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the directional derivative of the function $g(x, y) =3x^2+4xy$ at the point $A(0,1)$ in the direction towards the point $B(1,4).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The directional derivative $g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b)$ of a function $g(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf v$ is given by

$$
g'_{\mathbf u}(a,b) = \nabla g(a,b)\cdot\mathbf u
$$

where $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨1,4⟩-⟨0,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,3⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}⟨1,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}⟨1,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $\nabla g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+4xy),\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+4xy)⟩ \\  & =⟨6x+4y,\,4x⟩ \\ ∇g(0,1) & =⟨6\cdot 0+4\cdot 1,\,4\cdot 0⟩ \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(0,1) & =∇g(0,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}},\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{10} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: In what direction does the function $f (x, y) = \ln (x^2y)$ decrease most rapidly at the point $(2, 1)?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the direction opposite to that of its gradient.

So, we compute $-\nabla f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}y))\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}y))\text{ }j \\  & =-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\cdot 2xy\text{ }i-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}y}\cdot {x}^{2}j \\  & =-\frac{2}{x}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j \\ -∇f(2,1) & =-\frac{2}{2}\text{ }i-\frac{1}{1}\text{ }j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function decreases most rapidly in the direction of $- \, \mathbf i - \mathbf j.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Direction of Maximum Increase or Maximum Decrease of a Function

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Consider the function $g (x, y) = \ln \left(\sqrt {xy^3}\right).$ What is the rate of change of $g$ at the point $\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)$ in the direction in which the function increases most rapidly?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $\nabla g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)\!\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x{y}^{3}})),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}\cdot \frac{{y}^{3}}{2\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}},\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}\cdot \frac{3x{y}^{2}}{2\sqrt{x{y}^{3}}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2x},\,\frac{3}{2y}⟩ \\ ∇g(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}) & =⟨\frac{1}{2\cdot (\frac{1}{2})},\frac{3}{2\cdot (\frac{3}{2})}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)$ in the direction of $\nabla g\left(\dfrac 12, \dfrac 32 \right)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖∇g(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2})‖ & =‖⟨1,1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Rate of Change of a Function in a Given Direction
